papers.title: Mitohormesis linking metabolic dysfunction and neurodegeneration: implications for dementia and therapeutic strategies.
papers.summary: This paper discusses mitohormesis, a protective cellular response triggered by mild mitochondrial stress that can paradoxically improve cell resilience. It explores how this mechanism connects metabolic dysfunction to neurodegenerative processes seen in dementia. The paper also considers how mitohormesis might be targeted therapeutically to slow or prevent cognitive decline.
papers.why: Understanding mitohormesis and mitochondrial stress responses provides mechanistic context for mitophagy pathways in neurons, directly relevant to the mitochondrial quality control aspects of the PhD project.

papers.title: Intermittent theta-burst stimulation in ischemic stroke: a mitochondria-centered framework connecting microglial reprogramming and neuronal survival.
papers.summary: This paper proposes a conceptual framework suggesting that intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS), a non-invasive brain stimulation technique, helps treat ischemic stroke by targeting mitochondria. It argues that iTBS reprograms microglia (immune cells of the brain) in ways that reduce inflammation and support mitochondrial health. This mitochondrial support is proposed as a key mechanism linking microglial changes to improved neuronal survival after stroke.
papers.why: Although focused on stroke rather than neurodegeneration, this paper's mitochondria-centered mechanism linking microglial state to neuronal survival offers conceptual parallels relevant to mitophagy pathways in neurons that could inform your interneuron-focused research.

papers.title: Regulation of cellular proteostasis via mitochondrial protein import.
papers.summary: This paper (abstract not detailed) likely discusses how mitochondrial protein import machinery contributes to overall cellular protein quality control, or proteostasis. Mitochondria rely on precise import of nuclear-encoded proteins, and disruptions in this process can trigger stress responses that affect the broader proteome. Understanding this regulation is important because mitochondrial dysfunction and proteostasis collapse are linked to neurodegeneration and cellular aging.
papers.why: Mitochondrial protein import and proteostasis mechanisms are directly relevant to mitophagy regulation in neurons, since defects in import can trigger mitochondrial quality control pathways studied in this PhD project.

papers.title: Therapeutic Timing at Mitochondrial Redox-Autophagy-Mitophagy Checkpoints in Age-Related Hearing Loss.
papers.summary: This paper discusses how mitochondrial redox balance, autophagy, and mitophagy interact at critical checkpoints during the progression of age-related hearing loss. It proposes that the timing of therapeutic interventions targeting these pathways is crucial for effectiveness, since mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired clearance mechanisms change across different stages of aging. The authors likely argue for stage-specific strategies that modulate autophagic and mitophagic flux to preserve auditory cell function and delay hearing decline.
papers.why: The paper's detailed treatment of mitophagy and autophagy checkpoints tied to mitochondrial redox state offers mechanistic insights and potential methodological parallels relevant to studying similar pathways in aging neurons.
papers.figure: A schematic figure illustrating the proposed timeline of mitochondrial redox changes, autophagy induction, and mitophagy checkpoints across stages of age-related hearing loss.

papers.title: Lipophagy and lipid droplets in neurodegeneration.
papers.summary: This paper reviews lipophagy, the selective autophagic clearance of lipid droplets, and its role in neurodegenerative diseases. It discusses how impaired lipid droplet turnover in neurons and glia can contribute to toxic lipid accumulation and cellular dysfunction. The review likely connects defective lipophagy to pathways overlapping with mitophagy and broader autophagic dysfunction seen in conditions like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.
papers.why: Understanding lipophagy as a parallel selective autophagy pathway to mitophagy could reveal shared regulatory mechanisms relevant to neuronal and interneuron health in neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Manganese Dioxide Nanoparticles Protect PC12 Cells Against H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>-Induced Oxidative Stress Injury by Regulating PI3K/Akt-Mediated Autophagy.
papers.summary: This study tests whether manganese dioxide nanoparticles can shield PC12 neuronal-like cells from oxidative damage caused by hydrogen peroxide. The researchers found that these nanoparticles help regulate autophagy through the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, reducing cell injury. This suggests manganese dioxide nanoparticles could be a protective agent against oxidative stress-related neuronal damage.
papers.why: This paper's focus on autophagy regulation in neuron-like cells under oxidative stress is tangentially relevant background for mitophagy/autophagy mechanisms in neurons, though it uses a nanoparticle intervention and PC12 cell line rather than brain tissue, spatial omics, or interneuron/PNN contexts central to the project.

papers.title: Proteostasis (in)action: the role of co-pathologies in neurodegenerative disease.
papers.summary: This paper is a review discussing how protein homeostasis (proteostasis) networks, including autophagic and degradation pathways, can fail in neurodegenerative diseases. It likely explores how multiple co-occurring pathologies (e.g., protein aggregates, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation) interact to worsen disease progression. The abstract itself is sparse, suggesting a conceptual or review-style discussion rather than new experimental data.
papers.why: Understanding how proteostasis and co-pathologies intersect is directly relevant to mitophagy and autophagy dysfunction in neurons, a core mechanism underlying neurodegeneration in this PhD project.

papers.title: Nitrate-responsive Sialin2 couples stress granule assembly and clearance to maintain neuronal homeostasis.
papers.summary: This paper describes a protein called Sialin2 that responds to nitrate levels and helps control the formation and breakdown of stress granules, which are temporary clumps of RNA and proteins that cells make under stress. By linking the assembly and clearance of these granules, Sialin2 helps keep neurons functioning normally. The abstract suggests that disrupting this balance could harm neuronal health, pointing to a role for Sialin2 in cellular stress responses in the brain.
papers.why: Since stress granule clearance often intersects with autophagy pathways, this work could reveal a new mitophagy/autophagy-adjacent mechanism regulating neuronal proteostasis relevant to the PhD project's focus on neuronal clearance systems.
